nuevos.titulo_original: Luto prolongado é um transtorno mental? #Shorts
nuevos.descripcion:
Sentir dor, saudade e tristeza após a perda de alguém querido é normal e esperado. Mas, em alguns casos, o luto se prolonga e paralisa a pessoa enlutada, impedindo-a de seguir com a vida.

Desde 2022, o transtorno de luto prolongado integra o DSM-5, manual diagnóstico da Associação Americana de Psiquiatria. Para ser considerado um transtorno, os sintomas precisam persistir por mais de seis meses após a morte e causar prejuízo no dia a dia da pessoa.

O luto prolongado é tratável, e o acompanhamento de profissionais qualificados pode ajudar a pessoa a seguir em frente.

Neste Assunto da Semana, Mariana Varella explica como diferenciar o luto “saudável” do luto prolongado e quando procurar ajuda.

nuevos.descripcion:
In this episode, Peter welcomes back Jeff Cavaliere, a physical therapist, strength coach, and founder of ATHLEAN-X who has spent decades bridging the gap between rehabilitation, athletic performance, and strength training. Jeff begins by sharing how his experience working with professional athletes and managing his own injuries has shaped his approach to building strength and muscle while minimizing injury risk. He discusses how training should evolve as we age, particularly for those in their 40s, 50s, and beyond who want to continue making progress without compromising long-term joint health. Jeff explains why excessive training volume can be counterproductive and how to balance reps in reserve with training to failure to maximize results while managing fatigue and injury risk. He also explores the differences between training for aesthetics and functional performance, explaining why these goals are not necessarily at odds. The conversation then shifts to a muscle-by-muscle breakdown of effective exercises for building strength and hypertrophy. Jeff highlights common training mistakes, offers modifications for those dealing with pain or injury, and explains why often-neglected muscles deserve more attention.

nuevos.descripcion:
Can we slow aging in dogs and help them live longer, healthier lives? More than a decade ago, that question inspired the creation of the Dog Aging Project, which has grown from an ambitious idea into one of the largest studies of aging ever conducted in companion animals, with more than 55,000 dogs participating.

In this special presentation from the inaugural Animal Longevity Summit, Dr. Matt Kaeberlein shares the personal story behind the Dog Aging Project, beginning with his German Shepherd, Dobby, and the realization that discoveries from laboratory aging research might someday help our own dogs live longer.

Matt takes us through the project's history, from the first clinical trials of rapamycin in dogs to the challenges of building and sustaining a large-scale scientific effort. He also highlights some of the most interesting discoveries from the project and provides an update on TRIAD, the ongoing randomized, placebo-controlled clinical trial testing whether rapamycin can extend lifespan and improve healthspan in companion dogs.

Topics covered include:

How Dobby inspired Matt to pursue longevity research in dogs
The origins and evolution of the Dog Aging Project
How more than 55,000 dogs are helping scientists understand aging
Surprising associations between feeding frequency and age-related disease
What we're learning about canine dementia and brain aging
Why large dogs age faster but may not experience faster cognitive decline
The science behind rapamycin as a pot
